title.en: The Kayan Creation: The Tree from the Sun, the Creeper from the Moon
title.zh: 加揚創世：日生之樹與月生之藤

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kayan creation myth, sung in rhymed blank verse; recorded by Hose and McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), vol. II, the Kayan creation myth

summary.en: In the beginning there was a barren rock; rains bred moss, and worms aided by dung-beetles made soil by their castings. A sword-handle came down from the sun and became a great tree; from the moon came a creeper that hung from the tree and was mated with it through the action of the wind — and from this union were born the first human beings, Kaluban Gai and Kalubi Angai, incomplete, lacking legs and the lower half of their trunks, their entrails hanging loose and exposed.
summary.zh: 太初唯荒岩一塊；雨生苔蘚，蟲類得糞甲蟲之助，以其排洩物造土。一柄劍柄自太陽而降，化為大樹；自月亮來一藤蔓，懸於樹上，因風而與樹交合——由是誕生最早之人類卡魯班·該與卡魯比·安該；二形不完備，缺足與下半身，臟腑懸露於外。

sensitivity.note: Kayan creation myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912); colonial-era collection flagged; Bornean communities hold the heritage — paraphrase only.

narrative.en:
The Kayan creation myth, sung in rhymed blank verse by all branches of the Kayan people, is the great cosmogony of interior Borneo, recorded by Hose and McDougall in the opening years of the twentieth century.

BEGINNING: THE ROCK AND THE SOIL. In the beginning there was a barren rock. On this the rains fell and gave rise to moss, and the worms, aided by the dung-beetles, made soil by their castings — creation begins not with a god but with weather and the small labour of the lowliest creatures.

MIDDLE: THE TREE FROM THE SUN. Then a sword-handle (Haup Malat) came down from the sun and became a large tree; from the moon came a creeper, which hanging from the tree became mated with it through the action of the wind. From this union were born Kaluban Gai and Kalubi Angai, the first human beings, male and female — but they were incomplete, lacking the legs and the lower half of their trunks, so that their entrails hung loose and exposed. The world fills around them: leaves falling from the tree became the species of birds and winged insects; from the fallen fruits sprang the four-footed beasts; and resin oozing from the trunk gave rise to the domestic pig and fowl — two species distinguished, the myth says, by their understanding of matters that remain hidden from all others, even from human beings.

END: THE COMPLETION AND THE PEOPLES. The incomplete first humans produced Pengok Ngai and Katira Murei; Katira Murei bore a son, Batang Uta Tatai, who married Ajai Avai and begot the five ancestors of the existing peoples — Sijau Laho, Oding Lahang, Pabalan, Pliban and Tokong. Oding Lahang is claimed as ancestor by the Kayans and also by the Kenyahs and some Klemantan tribes; Tokong by the Sebops and the Punans — the genealogy of the myth is thus the charter of the interior's ethnic map.

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) makes humanity's completion a process, not an event (the legless first pair); (2) ties the human body to the tree and the sun-moon pair; (3) grants pigs and fowls a special secret knowledge that explains their use in divination; and (4) distributes the living peoples among five named ancestors. The myth's botany is deliberate: the sun supplies the tree, the moon the creeper, and the wind supplies the act of union, so that the first humans are the child of all three — solar stock, lunar climbing, and the breeze's joining. The incompleteness of Kaluban Gai and Kalubi Angai is the myth's signature: the first pair lack legs and the lower half of the trunk, their entrails exposed, and completion comes only through their descendants — humanity is finished by descent, not delivered ready-made. The same generative logic fills the world: leaves become birds and winged insects, fallen fruits become the four-footed beasts, and the resin of the trunk becomes the domestic pig and fowl, the two creatures credited with understanding what remains hidden from others — a charter, the recorders noted, for their use in divination. The genealogy then distributes the interior's peoples among the five sons of Batang Uta Tatai, so that the myth is at once a cosmogony and the ethnic map of Borneo sung in blank verse.
narrative.zh: 加揚創世神話以押韻之素體詩吟唱，流行於加揚諸支，由霍斯與麥克杜格爾於二十世紀初記錄。開篇：太初唯荒岩；雨生苔，蟲與糞甲蟲以其排洩物造土——創世始於天氣與至微生物之勞作，而非神明。中段：日降劍柄化大樹；月來之藤因風與樹交合，誕生首對不完備之人類（缺足與下半身，臟腑外露）。周遭世界隨之而生：落葉化為鳥與有翅之蟲，落果生四足獸，樹脂育出家豬與家雞——神話言此二者通曉連人類也隱而不知之事。結尾：不完備的首對人類生彭奧克·恩蓋與卡蒂拉·穆雷；其子巴當·烏塔·塔泰娶阿賈伊·阿瓦伊，生五支現存民族之祖——西兆·拉霍、奧丁·拉航、帕巴蘭、普利班、托貢。加揚人、肯雅人與部分克勒曼丹人奉奧丁·拉航為祖；塞博普人與普南人奉托貢為祖——神話之譜系即婆羅洲內陸族群地圖之憲章。功能：以『未完之人』立人性之漸成、以身體繫於樹與日月、以豬雞之秘知解釋占卜之用、以五祖分派現存民族。

functions: Makes human completion a process: the first pair lacks legs and lower trunks
Ties the human body to the sun-tree and the moon-creeper union
Grants pigs and fowls secret knowledge, explaining their use in divination
Distributes the living Bornean peoples among five named ancestors

variants.name: Kenyah variants
variants.summary: The Kenyahs claim Oding Lahang within a parallel genealogy headed by the supreme Bali Penylong, identified with the Kayan Laki Tenangan.

primary_sources.citation: Sung in rhymed blank verse among the Kayan; recorded in Hose & McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo, London 1912, vol. II.

secondary_sources.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo
secondary_sources.citation: Hose & McDougall 1912, London: Macmillan — vol. II, the mythology chapters.

passages.text: In the beginning there was a barren rock. On this the rains fell and gave rise to moss, and the worms, aided by the dung-beetles, made soil by their castings. Then a sword-handle came down from the sun and became a large tree. From the moon came a creeper, which hanging from the tree became mated with it through the action of the wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kayan creation myth in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

Leaves falling from the tree became the various species of birds and winged insects, and from the fallen fruits sprang the four-footed beasts; resin oozing from the trunk gave rise to the domestic pig and fowl, distinguished by their understanding of matters hidden from all others.

title.en: The Frog's Advice: Tokong and the Charter of Head-Hunting
title.zh: 青蛙之諫：托貢與獵首之憲章

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kayan/Klemantan myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the Tokong story

summary.en: Preparing to attack a village, Tokong is hailed by a frog crying 'cut through the neck.' The people, who had taken only their enemies' hair to adorn their shields, scoff — until the frog decapitates a small frog to demonstrate, and promises prosperity of every kind. Tokong carries away the heads of his enemies, and as the party returns home the padi grows from knee-high to full ears; head-hunting is adopted from that day as the rite that makes the crops and the household prosper.
summary.zh: 托貢正欲攻村，一蛙呼曰：『斬其頸！』眾人素來只取敵髮飾盾，皆嘲笑之——直至青蛙斬一小蛙以示範，並許諸般繁榮。托貢遂取敵首而歸；歸途經過田中，稻穀自膝高驟長至穗滿。自此獵首成為使莊稼興旺、家宅昌盛之禮。

sensitivity.note: Historical headhunting charter-myth, recorded 1912; presented as ethnographic record of a discontinued practice, framed with care.

passages.text: Once upon a time, when Tokong and his people were preparing to attack a village, he was addressed by the frog, who called out words meaning in the Sebop language 'cut through the neck.' At first the people, who hitherto had taken only the hair of their enemies to adorn their shields, scoffed at this advice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tokong story in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the frog assured them that the taking of heads would bring prosperity of every kind, and demonstrated the procedure by decapitating a small frog. Tokong carried away the heads of his enemies, and this was followed immediately by increased prosperity: as the party passed through their fields the padi grew very rapidly, from knee-high to full ears before they had passed through.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tokong story; not verbatim.

passages.text: The words of the frog thus came true, and Tokong and his people continued the new practice, and from them it was learned by others — the charter of the head-hunting rite and its promise of the harvest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tokong story; not verbatim.

title.en: Lafaang in the Sky: The Bridegroom Who Lost His Arm

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Long Kiput (Klemantan) star myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the story of Lafaang (Orion)

summary.en: The daughter of Palai (the constellation Pegasus) loves the Long Kiput youth Lafaang and brings him to the sky. Sky custom defeats him at every turn: food taken with fingers instead of a needle, trees that fall when the axe is merely laid at their feet — until a tree felled carelessly cuts off Lafaang's left arm, the very arm missing in the constellation Orion. Disgusted and homesick, he is let down to earth by a creeper with sugar-cane tops and banana roots, hears his newborn child cry as he descends, and plants the gifts in soil instead of throwing them — which is why, the myth says, cane and banana remain inferior wherever they grow, and why Orion still moves overhead, one-armed.
summary.zh: 帕拉伊（飛馬座）之女愛上隆基普青年拉方，引他上天。天界之俗處處敗他：以指代針取食、斧置樹腳樹即自倒——直到一棵粗心砍伐之樹墜落，斬斷拉方左臂——正是獵戶座所缺之臂。他厭倦思鄉，由藤蔓縋回地面，懷中帶著甘蔗梢與香蕉根；下降之際聽見新生兒啼哭而求回頭被拒。他將贈物種入土中而非擲地——神話言：故甘蔗香蕉至今低劣；而獵戶座仍缺臂巡天。

sensitivity.note: Star-myth with bride-taken-to-sky structure; Orion's missing arm fixed etiologically.

passages.text: The daughter of Palai fell in love with a Long Kiput youth, Lafaang, and invited him to ascend to the heavens, warning him that the customs of her celestial home were very different from those of earth. He found it difficult to conform: he put food into his mouth with his fingers instead of using a needle, and felled trees by chopping, when he was merely to lay the axe at their feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lafaang story in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: This breach of custom was punished by the fall of a tree that cut off Lafaang's left arm — the arm wanting in the constellation. Disgusted by these incidents, he made up his mind to return to his own people; his wife let him down to earth by a long creeper, giving him sugar-cane tops and banana roots previously unknown to men, and he heard the cry of his new-born child as he descended but was not allowed to return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lafaang story; not verbatim.

passages.text: Told to throw the gifts on the ground, he planted them carefully in soil instead; the plants grew up inferior, and such they have remained wherever they have spread. Lafaang died among his own people on earth, but the bright constellation that bears his name and shape still moves across the heavens, reminding men of his journey to the world above the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lafaang story; not verbatim.

title.en: Usaï the Giant: Why the Sky Is Far Away

region.en: Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河流域（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Klemantan myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the story of Usaï

summary.en: At one time the sky was close to the earth; but one day Usaï, a giant working sago with a wooden mallet, accidentally struck his mallet against the sky, and since then the sky has been far out of man's reach. The rest of the myth follows the giant's grief down the Baram: the dammed river that drowns his wife, the weeping stations that name every rapid, his cut-down death at Miri with 'my brains are sago, my liver is tobacco,' and the mosquitoes of his day, big as fowls, hewn small by the people.
summary.zh: 昔天低近地；一日巨人烏賽舂西谷米，木杵誤擊於天——自此天高而人不可及。神話續敘巨人順巴蘭江而下之悲：築壩引水而妻溺亡；沿江哭泣之處各成灘名；至米里被伐如樹而亡——遺言曰『吾腦為西谷、吾肝為菸草』；其世之蚊大如雞，為眾人斬小。

sensitivity.note: Sky-lifting motif (cf. Maui, Reushi); landscape etiology of the Baram rapids.

passages.text: At one time the sky was close to the earth, but one day Usaï, a giant, when working sago with a wooden mallet accidentally struck his mallet against the sky; since which time the sky has been far up out of the reach of man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Usaï story in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Building a dam to catch a prawn for his wife, Usaï saw the dam give way and his wife drowned in the rush of water; he waded weeping down the Baram, and his stations of grief gave the river its named rapids — weeping anew at every bend where he found her coat, her waist-cloth, or nothing at all, until the sea was only knee-deep to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Usaï story; not verbatim.

passages.text: At Miri the people took him for a great tree and hewed him down; blood poured from his foot, and he spoke: 'I am about to die. My brains are sago, my liver is tobacco. Where my head falls there the people will have much knowledge, where my feet lie will be the ignorant ones.' He fell with a mighty crash, head toward the sea; a thousand Miris were killed by the fall, and the mosquitoes of his day, big as fowls, were hewn into small pieces — so that now they are the smallest of animals, but their bite is still painful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Usaï story; not verbatim.

title.en: Simpang Impang and the Wind-Spirit: The Flood, the Half-Man, the Compensation
title.zh: 半身人與風靈：洪水、半人與賠償

region.zh: 婆羅洲巴唐盧帕爾流域（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Iban (Sea Dayak) myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the Iban story of Simpang Impang

summary.en: Men who cut up a python for cooking bring on a deluge; all the land is covered and only the peak of Tiang Laju stands above the flood, with one woman, a dog, a rat and a few small animals. The woman, taking a hint from a creeper warmed by friction, produces fire by rubbing wood; lacking a husband she takes the creeper as mate and bears a son who is only half a human being — one arm, one leg, one eye: Simpang Impang. When the wind-spirit scatters the rat's padi the half-boy demands compensation at the house of the wind, outlasts the spirit's ordeal contests with the help of fish, swift and ant, burns the wind-house with his father the fire-drill, and wins the price: 'I'll make you a whole man with two arms and two legs and two eyes.'
summary.zh: 人們誤斬巨蟒而炊，招致大洪水；大地盡沒，唯蒂昂·拉尤峰出於水面，一婦人攜犬、鼠及小獸登峰。婦人見藤蔓摩擦生暖而悟，鑽木取火；無夫，遂以藤為伴，產下半身之子——一臂一腿一目：半身人辛邦·因邦。風靈吹散鼠之稻穀，半身人前往風之居所索償；得魚、雨燕、螞蟻之助連勝神判，再以生父鑽火器焚風屋——風靈終允賠償：『我讓你成為完人，兩臂兩腿兩目。』

sensitivity.note: Iban composite myth (flood + quest + fable); Hose notes its heterogeneous, fun-loving character.

passages.text: Some people came upon a huge python in the jungle and, taking it for a log, sat on it and wounded it; heavy rain fell for days and days, till all the land was covered with water and only the top of Tiang Laju stood out above the flood, with one woman, a dog, a rat and a few small animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iban story of Simpang Impang in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The woman, taking the hint from a creeper warmed by friction against a tree, rubbed the creeper hard on a piece of wood and so for the first time produced fire; having no husband she took the creeper for her mate, and gave birth to a son who was but one-half of a human being — one arm, one leg, one eye — Simpang Impang.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iban story; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the wind-spirit scattered the padi grain in dispute with the rat, Simpang Impang demanded his corn back at the house of the wind; helped by the fish, the swift and the ant through the spirit's contests of diving, jumping and blow-pipe, and armed at last with his father the fire-drill, he burned the wind-spirit's house, and the spirit paid compensation — 'I'll make you a whole man with two arms and two legs and two eyes' — and did as asked for the tree and the lake that had sent messages with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iban story; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mouse-Deer and the Tortoise: 'Please Throw Me in the River'
title.zh: 鼠鹿與水龜：『請把我丟進河裏』

region.en: Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河流域（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kenyah fable recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the Kenyah fable of the mouse-deer and the tortoise

summary.en: The mouse-deer Plandok gives the tortoise Kelap a leg up the fruit-tree and abandons him; caught by the household as the thief, Kelap begs for each punishment — fire ('last time they left one side untouched'), the cane-press ('last time they squeezed only one side') — and weeps only at the river. Thrown in, he surfaces: 'That's alright, this is my home.' The villagers try to poison the water with tuba, but one man uses the tortoise's back for a stone, and Kelap sinks his back little by little until they think the river is rising and give up.
summary.zh: 鼠鹿普蘭多克扶水龜柯拉普上果樹而棄之；柯拉普被屋中人當賊擒獲，對各種刑罰皆討饒求之——火刑（『上次只燒了一面』）、蔗壓（『上次只壓了一面』）——唯獨怕被丟入河中而啼哭。眾人將其拋入河中，他浮出水面：『沒錯，這就是我的家。』村民欲以毒藤毒水，一人竟以其背為砧杵搗毒藤；柯拉普讓背慢慢下沉，眾人以為河水漲了，只好作罷。

sensitivity.note: Classic trickster fable (punishment-inversion type); also performed as social parable among the Kenyahs.

passages.text: Plandok the mouse-deer gives Kelap the tortoise a leg up the laden fruit-tree; Kelap throws down all the fruit, cannot get down, and is caught by the people of the house as the thief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kenyah fable in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brought to punishment, Kelap begs for every fate but the river: 'please put me in the fire; last time they only half did the thing and left one side untouched'; 'please squeeze me in the press; last time they squeezed only one side of me.' So they throw him into the river, and he surfaces calling that this is his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kenyah fable; not verbatim.

passages.text: The people resolve to poison the water with tuba; one man, taking Kelap's back for a stone, beats his tuba upon it, and Kelap sinks his back lower and lower till the water covers it — 'the water's rising, it's no good trying to poison the river' — and the people go home defeated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kenyah fable; not verbatim.

title.en: Laki Tenangan: The Fatherly God Above All Departments
title.zh: 拉基·特南安：超越諸職司的慈父之神

region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸加揚之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kayan religious tradition recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the gods of the Kayans

summary.en: Above the Kayan departmental gods stands Laki Tenangan, 'more powerful than all the rest, to whom are assigned no special functions' — a beneficent, fatherly god who protects mankind, whose identity the Kayan freely admits with the supreme gods of the Klemantans and Kenyahs. Prayers are carried to him by the souls of slaughtered pigs and fowls, with fire and ascending smoke; an old woman praying for her sick child says: 'Make my child live that I may bring him up with me in my occupations... If I put you above my head, all men look up to me as to a high cliff.'
summary.zh: 加揚諸職司神之上，立著拉基·特南安——『權能勝過其餘眾神，而不司任何特定職務』——仁慈如父、護佑人類之神；加揚人坦然承認他與克勒曼丹人、肯雅人之至上神同為一體。禱詞由被宰豬雞之魂傳達，並輔以火與升煙；老嫗為病兒禱曰：『讓我的孩子活下來，好讓我帶著他一起勞作……若我將您置於我頭頂之上，萬人都會仰望我，如仰望高崖。』

sensitivity.note: Supreme-god theology recorded 1912; Hose & McDougall compare its 'catholicity' across tribes.

passages.text: Beside or above all the departmental gods is Laki Tenangan, a god more powerful than all the rest, to whom are assigned no special functions; he seems to preside over the company of lesser gods much as Zeus ruled the lesser gods of the Greeks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912), the Kayan gods; not verbatim.

passages.text: Laki Tenangan is conceived as beneficent and fatherly; the Kayan admits his identity with Pa Silong and Bali Penylong, the supreme gods of the Klemantans and Kenyahs — a catholicity which, the recorders note, gives the Kayan religion a claim to rank very high among religious systems.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Prayers are transmitted to him by the souls of domestic pigs or fowls, one of which is always killed and charged to carry the prayer, while fire and ascending smoke establish the communication. The supplicant cries: 'Make my child live that I may bring him up with me in my occupations. You are above all men. Protect us from whatever sickness is abroad. If I put you above my head, all men look up to me as to a high cliff.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912), the recorded prayer; not verbatim.

title.en: The Trusty Messengers: Omen Birds and the Sacrifice of Beads
title.zh: 忠實的信使：占卜鳥與斷珠之祭

region.en: Kayan and Kenyah country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸加揚與肯雅之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Religious practice recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the omen birds and sacrificial rites

summary.en: The Kayans seek to read in the behaviour of the omen birds and in the entrails of slaughtered pigs and fowls the way the gods respond to prayer: 'they regard the true omen birds as the trusty messengers of the gods.' Bad omens are retried with fresh victims until satisfactory ones come; and the sacrifice is real deprivation — the pigs stuck upon stakes before the altar-post are left to rot, a woman whose child's recovery stays unanswered will break a bead of great value, or cut off her hair.
summary.zh: 加揚人在占卜鳥之行止與被宰豬雞之腸中，讀取諸神對禱告的回應——『他們視真正的占卜鳥為諸神忠實的信使』。凶兆則以新的犧牲重占，直至得吉；而犧牲是真實的剝奪——釘於祭柱前木樁上的豬任其腐爛；若病兒痊癒之禱未蒙應允，婦人會折斷貴重之珠，或剪下自己的頭髮。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic record of living religious practice (1912); paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: The Kayans seek to read in the behaviour of the omen birds and in the entrails of the slaughtered pigs and fowls indications of the way in which the gods respond to their prayers; for they regard the true omen birds as the trusty messengers of the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: If the omens first obtained are bad, more fowls and pigs are usually killed and omens again observed; in an important matter, as the illness of a beloved child, the process may be repeated many times until satisfactory omens are forthcoming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The slaughtering is regarded as sacrifice in the ordinary sense — an offering of some valued possession: the pigs stuck upon stakes before the altar-post are left to rot; a woman will break a bead of great value when her prayers for the restoration of her child's health remain unanswered, or on such an occasion may cut off her hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Kayan Pantheon: Gods of War, Life, Madness and the Ferry of Souls
title.zh: 加揚神譜：戰神、生命之神、瘋神與渡魂者

region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸加揚之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Religious tradition recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the gods of the Kayans

summary.en: The Kayans recognise gods presiding over the great departments of life: the god of war, Toh Bulu; three gods of life, Laki Ju Urip, Laki Makatan Urip and Laki Kalisai Urip; the god of thunder and storms, Laki Balari, with his wife Obeng Doh; the god of fire, Laki Pesong; the harvest gods Anyi Lawang and Laki Ivong; the god of lakes and rivers, Urai Uka; Balanan the god of madness; Toh Kiho the god of fear; and Laki Katira Murei and Laki Jup Urip, who conduct the souls of the dead to Hades — the minor gods, Hose suggests, perhaps deified ancestors, their names the names of Kayan grandfathers.
summary.zh: 加揚人奉眾神分掌人生諸大事：戰神托赫·布盧；三位生命之神（拉基·朱·烏里普、拉基·瑪卡丹·烏里普、拉基·卡利賽·烏里普）；雷暴之神拉基·巴拉里及其妻奧本·多赫；火神拉基·珀松；穀神安宜·拉旺與拉基·伊旺；湖河之神烏萊·烏卡；瘋神巴拉南；懼神托赫·基霍；以及引亡魂至冥府的拉基·卡蒂拉·穆雷與拉基·朱普·烏里普——小神或為受尊崇之祖先，其名即加揚祖父之名。

sensitivity.note: Pantheon record; the ancestor-deification hypothesis is the recorders' interpretation.

passages.text: The Kayans recognise a number of gods that preside over great departments of their lives and interests: the god of war, Toh Bulu; three gods of life; the god of thunder and storms, Laki Balari, and his wife Obeng Doh; the god of fire, Laki Pesong; gods of the harvest; a god of the lakes and rivers; Balanan, the god of madness; Toh Kiho, the god of fear; and two gods who conduct the souls of the dead to Hades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912), the Kayan pantheon; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some of these gods are distinctly friendly, others — the gods of madness and fear — terrible and malevolent; while the god of thunder and the conductors of souls are neither. The names of many minor deities are proper personal names in common use, and the title Laki is the respectful title of grandfathers — suggesting that these minor gods may be deified ancestors of great chiefs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Measuring the Stars with a Bamboo of Water: Dayak Sky-Lore
title.zh: 以竹筒量星：達雅克星空之學

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Astronomical tradition recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the constellations of the Borneans

summary.en: Most Borneans are familiar with the principal constellations and name them from resemblances to men, animals and objects. The Long Kiputs call the great square of Pegasus 'Palai,' the padi storehouse; the Pleiades they call a well; the constellation of Aldebaran, a pig's jaw. They measure a star's altitude by filling a tall bamboo vessel with water, inclining it until it points to the star, then measuring the water-line — an indigenous astrolabe of bamboo and water.
summary.zh: 婆羅洲人多識主要星座，依其似人似獸似物而命名。隆基普人稱飛馬座大方形為『帕拉伊』——稻倉；稱昴星團為井；稱畢宿座為豬顎。他們以高竹筒盛水，傾筒對星，再直立量水面之高——此即以竹與水製成的本土星儀。

sensitivity.note: Ethnoastronomy record; the sowing season is set by these observations.

passages.text: Most of the Borneans are familiar with the principal constellations, and name them in accordance with the resemblances they discover to men, animals, and other objects; some of the tribes determine the arrival of the season for sowing padi by the observation of the stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912), the constellations; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Long Kiputs name the great square of Pegasus Palai, the padi storehouse; the Pleiades they call a well; and the constellation of which Aldebaran is a member they call a pig's jaw. They measure the altitude of a star by filling a tall bamboo vessel with water, inclining it until it points directly to the star, and then setting it upright again, and measuring the height at which the surface of the water remaining stands above its floor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
